name: Metadata and Ontologies
title: Metadata and Ontologies
answer: Metadata and ontologies in research data and repositories concern the structured descriptions that make datasets, models, and papers findable, comparable, and reusable. This includes descriptive, administrative, and structural metadata, as well as formal ontologies that define classes, properties, and relationships within a domain. The work spans schema design, vocabulary alignment, and the application of standards such as Dublin Core, DataCite, and OWL. It also covers how repositories expose metadata through APIs and harvesters, and how ontologies support semantic search and data integration across collections.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Metadata and ontologies in research data and repositories concern the structured descriptions that make datasets, models, and papers findable, comparable, and reusable. This includes descriptive, administrative, and structural metadata, as well as formal ontologies that define classes, properties, and relationships within a domain. The work spans schema design, vocabulary alignment, and the application of standards such as Dublin Core, DataCite, and OWL. It also covers how repositories expose metadata through APIs and harvesters, and how ontologies support semantic search and data integration across collections.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: This work runs on repository platforms, triple stores, and graph databases that store metadata records and ontology graphs. Common components include SPARQL endpoints, OAI-PMH harvesters, and schema registries, along with indexing services that make metadata searchable. Many repositories use relational databases for transactional metadata and separate graph stores for ontology reasoning. The infrastructure also includes validation services that check metadata against schemas and ontologies before records are published.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done by first eliciting domain concepts from researchers and existing data dictionaries, then formalizing them into classes and properties with clear definitions and constraints. Metadata records are created or transformed to conform to these schemas, often through crosswalks that map fields between standards. Ontology development typically follows iterative cycles of modeling, review by domain experts, and testing against real repository records. Automated extraction and linking tools can propose metadata from papers and datasets, but human curation remains central for accuracy and semantic consistency.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk in this area center on provenance, attribution, and the persistence of identifiers. Metadata records must record who created a dataset, what license applies, and how the data was derived, because incomplete or incorrect metadata can lead to misuse or misattribution. Ontologies carry governance risks when terms are ambiguous, change meaning over time, or encode biased classifications. Versioning, change logs, and community stewardship are common practices to manage these risks, and repositories often require metadata to include provenance fields before deposit.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward more automated metadata generation from full-text papers and dataset contents, with ontologies used to reconcile terms across disciplines. Knowledge graphs built from repository metadata are becoming more common as a way to connect datasets, models, and publications. There is also growing interest in machine-readable data management plans and persistent, resolvable identifiers for every object and concept. The likely direction is tighter coupling between ontologies and repository workflows, so that semantic validation happens at deposit time rather than as a later cleanup step.
